title: Tool-provider engine: lifecycle registry with MCP and memory providers
description: Build the typed tool-provider capability family over the central tools registry. Providers declare a plugin manifest, lifecycle/health, and discover executable ToolEntry values. Add adapters for memory.Manager and configured MCP servers, perform MCP initialize/tools-list/tools-call, register handlers atomically with collision rollback, translate available entries to ai-sdk core.ToolSet, and wire consumers so registered tools are actually callable rather than dead daemon fields.
design: internal/tools owns Provider and ProviderRegistry; Provider is a typed domain contract and uses the shared plugin manifest/lifecycle vocabulary. The registry owns provider registration and tool indexing while the capability host orchestrates cross-family lifecycle. Memory is adapted without changing internal/memory concurrent work. MCP provider wraps the existing stdio transport without modifying its concurrent implementation, adds protocol client behavior in new files, prefixes/sanitizes server tool names deterministically, and retains original MCP names for calls. Never advertise a tool on an execution path that cannot invoke its handler; explicitly proxy or omit tools across subprocess/NATS boundaries.
acceptance_criteria: Provider registration is atomic and rejects duplicate provider/tool IDs without partial state. Start/discovery failure rolls back tools and lifecycle; stop removes availability and shuts providers down in reverse order. Memory provider tools appear in the central registry and execute through memory.Manager. A fake MCP server proves initialize, initialized notification where supported, tools/list discovery, tools/call execution, JSON-RPC errors, shutdown, and name mapping. Available tools convert to valid ai-sdk core.ToolSet and are used by the gateway conversational loop and supported agent execution paths; unsupported remote paths do not advertise unusable handlers. Configuration creates providers through typed factories. Focused/race tests, lint, task check, and fresh adversarial review pass subject only to documented concurrent baseline failures.
notes:
Implemented typed provider.Engine + provider.Registry capability family; atomic central RegisterBatch/Unregister; dependency-ordered start/discovery, bounded rollback, retryable failed cleanup, reverse stop and health aggregation. Added memory.Manager adapter and lifecycle-managed MCP adapter with initialize/list/call, deterministic ASCII name mapping, original-name dispatch, tool errors, resource text and multimodal preservation. Composition uses typed config factory, omits unsupported HTTP/unknown transports, registers the family with capabilityHost, defers gateways until host+daemon startup, shuts memory down, builds validated ai-sdk ToolSets, uses independent 8-step chat loop, and exposes handlers only to Telegram chat/in-process agents. Focused race tests pass; scoped lint 0; fresh final adversarial review 0 findings. task check passes every package except known concurrent internal/gateway /spawn tests. Dependency abg.17.16 remains independently in progress.
Implementation and review are complete; Beads closure is intentionally deferred because required transport issue archie-core-abg.17.16 is still open. Close without --force when that dependency completes.
close_reason: Blocking dependency abg.17.16 closed; tool-provider engine work was already implementation-complete and previously reviewed clean.

title: Capability host: manifests, lifecycle, health, and typed family installation
description: Replace the inert metadata-only daemon plugin inventory with a capability host that validates plugin manifests and coordinates lifecycle without adding generic domain hooks. The host owns module identity/API compatibility/dependency ordering/start/health/stop state; typed family registries remain responsible for capability registration. Wire it into archied startup/shutdown and expose status without passing *daemon.Daemon to plugins.
design: Keep plugin.Plugin exactly Name/Version. Add a validated Manifest and lifecycle vocabulary in internal/plugin plus a Host that manages manifests and lifecycle only. Capability packages receive narrow typed registrars; the host must not become an any-typed service locator. Start in dependency order, roll back a partially failed start, stop in reverse order, isolate panics/errors, and return immutable health snapshots. Preserve existing Yaegi loading through an adapter or manifest synthesis for metadata-only legacy plugins.
acceptance_criteria: Manifest validation covers stable ID, semantic version, host API compatibility, declared capability kinds, dependencies, permissions, and optional config schema. Duplicate IDs, missing dependencies, cycles, incompatible API versions, and invalid manifests fail deterministically. Host lifecycle tests prove dependency-ordered start, rollback, reverse stop, health aggregation, idempotent shutdown, and panic/error isolation. archied owns one host and starts/stops it. plugin.Plugin remains metadata-only and architecture tests pass. task check and lint are green apart from explicitly identified concurrent baseline failures; fresh adversarial review has no surviving findings.
notes: Implemented strict manifest validation, dependency-ordered lifecycle, bounded/retryable rollback cleanup, reverse shutdown, health snapshots, legacy metadata adapter, and archied composition. Removed divergent daemon PluginRegistry. TDD focused tests, race tests, lint, formatting, and independent adversarial re-review all pass with zero surviving findings. Repository-wide task check remains separately subject to concurrent gateway work.
close_reason: Capability host, manifest/lifecycle, composition, enforcement tests, and adversarial remediation complete

title: Built-in memory tool actions: add, replace, remove

add(target_section, content) appends to or creates a named section
replace(target_section, substring, replacement) finds first match of substring in section and replaces it

Substring matching is exact, case-sensitive by default (configurable)

Size bounds are checked before any write (reject if would exceed max file size)

title: Built-in memory tool: file-backed persistent memory

acceptance_criteria:
Built-in provider lives in internal/memory/builtin package
MEMORY.md stores persistent agent memory (facts, preferences, state across sessions)
USER.md stores user-provided context (background, instructions, preferences)

design: THE BOUNDARY IS THE POINT. The existing layering rule (recorded in the chat-system-prompt-design memory) is that PersonaRegistry is the style layer only and rules live in the template, so switching persona cannot strip the agent's rules or tool inventory. SOUL inherits exactly that constraint: it owns identity, name, register and warmth, and must not be able to touch core_rules -- otherwise 'be terse' in a SOUL silently disarms the no-fabrication rules. Steal from Hermes: is_legacy_template_soul upgrades untouched scaffolding in place but never overwrites a SOUL the user actually edited. This is the first of the three identity layers agreed with Sam on 2026-07-30: invariants (template, nobody edits at runtime) / SOUL (user-authored) / representation (curator-derived, proposes only).
acceptance_criteria: A user can name their agent and define its personality by editing a file, with no rebuild and no restart. An absent or empty SOUL falls back to the shipped default identity. SOUL cannot weaken the invariants: <instruction_precedence>, <core_rules>, the <tools> block and <env> stay in the template and remain unreachable from SOUL, enforced by a test. title: Audit the remaining golangci-lint autofix changes in 6d4e0be
description: Commit 6d4e0be applied a golangci-lint --fix batch across 8 files. One of the eight was a behaviour regression: the errorlint fix in internal/tools/builtin/grep.go rewrote 'if exitErr, ok := err.(*exec.ExitError); ok && exitErr.ExitCode() == 1' into 'errors.As(err, &exitErr)' and dropped the exit-code check, so any ripgrep failure (bad pattern, unreadable path) was reported to the model as 'no matches found' -- the agent would state a file contains nothing on the strength of a search that never ran. Fixed in 782510d. The other seven changes were eyeballed as benign (naked return expanded, err != ctx.Err() -> errors.Is) but were never verified individually. A one-in-eight regression rate does not justify trusting the remainder on inspection alone.
acceptance_criteria: Each remaining changed hunk in 6d4e0be is reviewed against its pre-fix behaviour, specifically for predicates that were narrowed or widened. internal/channels/telegram/model.go, internal/infrastructure/configuration/discovery.go, internal/tools/builtin/find.go, internal/tools/builtin/shell.go and the touched test files are covered. Any behaviour change found gets a regression test in the style of TestGrepReportsSearchFailureRatherThanNoMatches.
notes:
AUDIT COMPLETE. Per-hunk verdicts against pre-fix behaviour:

- telegram/model.go (nakedret expansion): return order matches the declaration, and no defer mutates the results, so the expansion is behaviour-neutral. Two strings and three bools mean a transposed pair would have compiled silently, so it is now pinned by TestParseModelRestReturnsDeclaredValuesInOrder. Writing that test surfaced an unrelated P1 regression from 651de0a -- archie-core-0d6, fixed here.
- configuration/discovery.go ((path string, yaml bool, ok bool) -> (path string, yaml, ok bool)): type-identical signature reshuffle, no semantic content.
- tools/builtin/find.go (err != ctx.Err() -> !errors.Is(err, ctx.Err())): behaviour-neutral. Verified on go1.26 that errors.Is(err, nil) is false for non-nil err, so with a live context the new predicate still means err != nil. With a cancelled context the walk returns ctx.Err() unwrapped, so identity and errors.Is agree. The audit did expose that this branch is unreachable in practice and cancellation is reported as 'no matches found' -- pre-existing, filed as archie-core-ts9.
- tools/builtin/shell.go (err.(*exec.ExitError) -> errors.As): NOT the grep failure. The original had no companion condition to drop -- the exit code is read inside the branch, not used to gate it -- and the ctx.Err() timeout check already runs first. Widening to wrapped ExitErrors is unreachable since cmd.Run returns them unwrapped. The branch had no test at all, so TestShellReportsExitCodeRatherThanAGenericError now covers it.
- loader_test.go, pluginextract/*.go, secretextract/*.go: blank-line insertions only.
- read_test.go ((cwd string, params string) -> (cwd, params string)): type-identical.
- webui_test.go ("GET" -> http.MethodGet): same constant value.

One-in-eight held: the batch itself had exactly the one regression already fixed in 782510d. The lint-driven refactor in 651de0a, however, carried a second regression of the same family, which suggests the review discipline belongs on structural extractions as much as on --fix batches.

title: Decide and implement the TOML write strategy
description: Settle how setup persists config before any prompting code is written; everything else depends on it. BurntSushi/toml loses comments on re-marshal, and config.example.toml carries substantial inline documentation users are meant to read and edit by hand. Options: (a) generate a fresh commented config from a template on first run and only line-patch specific keys on re-run; (b) full re-marshal and accept losing comments; (c) adopt a comment-preserving TOML editor.
design:
Decision: text-based line patching, not decode/re-marshal, not a comment-preserving TOML AST library (none exist for Go that are safe to depend on).

New package internal/infrastructure/configuration/tomlwrite:
- Apply(src []byte, edits []Edit) ([]byte, error): for each {Table, Key, Value} edit, finds an active "key = value" line in that table and replaces just the value (preserving indent + trailing inline comment); else finds a commented "# key = value" line in that table, uncomments the table header and the line; else appends the key at the end of the table's content (or appends a brand new [table] section at EOF if the table doesn't exist at all, active or commented). Lines not named by an edit are copied through byte-for-byte.
- Generate(template, edits) is Apply against configtemplate.Example (config.example.toml embedded at the module root via configtemplate.go, since go:embed can't reach outside its own directory tree -- this keeps config.example.toml the single source of truth instead of a second copy, which is exactly the drift bug this epic exists to fix).
- Value callers pre-render TOML literals; String() and Ref(engine,key) helpers cover the two shapes setup needs (quoted strings, secret.SecretRef inline tables). Deliberately does not import internal/secret -- it edits text, not Go values.

Trade-off: only understands single-line scalar/inline-table values. Does not handle multi-line arrays or [[array-of-tables]] (e.g. [[repos]]) -- those aren't setup's targets and must not be routed through this patcher.

Tests (internal/infrastructure/configuration/tomlwrite/tomlwrite_test.go) cover: active-key replace preserving trailing comment, active inline-table replace, commented-table uncomment-one-key-leave-siblings-commented, append into existing active table, append brand-new table, byte-identical-elsewhere on a single edit, byte-identical-elsewhere across two sequential runs (the rs9 acceptance criterion), and a full run against the real config.example.toml verified to decode via BurntSushi/toml and round-trip bot_user/forge.token correctly.

`go build ./...` and `task check` pass clean; no other files touched.
acceptance_criteria: The chosen strategy is documented with its trade-off. A first run produces a config a human can read and hand-edit afterwards. A second run changing one value leaves every other line, including comments, byte-identical -- asserted by a test. No strategy is adopted that silently discards user edits.
close_reason: text-based line patcher implemented in internal/infrastructure/configuration/tomlwrite; template embedded via configtemplate.go; tests pass, task check clean

description: Move config generation out of install.sh and into the daemon as 'archied setup', so the thing that writes config.toml is the same code that reads it. install.sh currently hand-rolls TOML and has already drifted from the schema once: it hardcoded the GitHub token key and the Gitea host, so a Gitea install produced a config naming a token the installer never wrote. design: Port from tau: the CLI/app split behind a SetupPrompter interface so business logic is UI-agnostic and testable without a terminal; plain-stdio Select and hidden ReadSecret (golang.org/x/term) racing ctx.Done for Ctrl+C -- no TUI dependency; atomic temp+rename writes. DIVERGENCE FROM TAU: tau surgically patches YAML nodes to preserve comments. archie uses BurntSushi/toml, which does not preserve comments across a decode/encode round trip, so a full re-marshal would destroy config.example.toml's documentation. Decide this explicitly -- see the child issue. Secrets differ too: archie already has secret.SecretRef{engine,key} indirection, so setup writes the reference into TOML and the value into the env engine's store; that is archie's equivalent of tau's config.yaml/auth.yaml split and should be used rather than reinvented.
acceptance_criteria: install.sh no longer generates config.toml; it invokes archied setup. Setup is idempotent and re-runnable against an existing config without clobbering unrelated settings. Every config it writes passes configuration.Validate, verified by a test that runs setup non-interactively and validates the output. Secrets never reach config.toml or argv: config holds a secret reference, the value goes to the env file at 0600 via atomic write. Prompts for secrets do not echo. A non-TTY invocation without sufficient input fails with a clear message rather than writing a partial config.

title: Trigger accounting: curator output must not feed its own trigger

title: Curator runtime: persistent loop with idle cooldown

acceptance_criteria: A curator with pending input runs without waiting for its next interval; an idle curator consumes no meaningful CPU and wakes on new input. Cooldown and check-in interval are configurable per curator. Loop timing is tested with a fake clock, not wall-clock sleeps. Shutdown is clean and bounded: an in-flight curator pass is cancelled via context and the daemon does not block indefinitely on it. A panicking curator is recovered and isolated from other curators and from the agent loop.

A registry controls registration, discovery, and shutdown ordering, and defines failure isolation. Curators receive a narrow typed registrar and only the host services their declared capability requires -- never *daemon.Daemon or an untyped hook map. internal/plugin/architecture_test.go recognises curator as a conforming engine family.

title: [EPIC] Curator engine: persistent memory-reasoning agent loops
description: Introduce curators as their own engine family: long-running agent loops that reason over memory and perform small maintenance tasks, rather than one hardcoded background job. A curator is defined by a check-in interval, a tool set, and (once the memory engine family lands) an attached memory engine. It runs persistently while there is input and backs off to a cooldown when idle. Ship two reference curators -- a skill curator and a persistent-session-memory curator -- so the interface is proven against two consumers rather than designed around one.
design: Modelled on Honcho's dreamer (/work/clones/honcho/src/dreamer). Two findings from that source worth carrying: (1) the split between a cheap hot-path extractor and an expensive sampled reasoner, so agentic cost is never paid per message; (2) surprisal-based sampling to choose which memories deserve attention, implemented over embeddings via interchangeable strategies including a k-NN graph random walk. Note Archie has no embedding capability today, so any surprisal-style sampling is gated behind adding one.
acceptance_criteria: Curator is a conforming engine family per ARCHITECTURE.md 'Plugin engine rule (strict)': typed contract, owning registry/manager, start/health/stop, narrow typed host access. Curators are registered and configured declaratively, not hardcoded. The runtime supports persistent operation under load and cooldown when idle, with intervals configurable per curator. Both reference curators run against the shipped defaults. Curator activity is observable: what ran, when, what it changed, and why. A curator failure is isolated and never takes down the daemon or a chat turn.

The contract must express real memory operations (write observation, query, list, forget), not just Name/Version.
acceptance_criteria: Memory is a typed engine family with an owning registry/manager, start/health/stop lifecycle, and narrow typed host access, satisfying every invariant in ARCHITECTURE.md 'Plugin engine rule (strict)' and passing internal/plugin/architecture_test.go. The builtin file-writing store is the shipped default engine and remains the behaviour when nothing is configured. At least one external engine is implementable against the contract without changes to the agent loop or gateway. Engine selection and per-engine settings are configurable, validated, and documented. title: chat: mid-conversation context loss, undiagnosed
description:
Reported from a real Telegram transcript (29 Jul, ~09:47 AEST / 23:47 UTC 28
Jul). Turn 3 of a coherent conversation was answered with a fresh greeting as
though no history existed; turn 4 was coherent again.

Ruled out by evidence:
- Not two processes racing the bot token. docker compose ps on carina shows a
  single archied container.
- Not a restart. That container had 43h uptime spanning the whole exchange.
- Not history compression. DefaultCompressionConfig protects the first 3 and
  last 20 messages and triggers at 50% of a 128k window; there were three
  messages.
- Not a canned greeting. No such string exists in the codebase, so the reply
  was model-generated from little or no history.
- Not the session-key namespace split fixed in 96ab167: the deployed image
  predates the session lifecycle commands entirely.

Blocked on evidence, now unblocked: chat turns were completely unlogged (76
log lines covered two days, none a conversation). 96ab167 adds a "chat turn"
log line carrying session id, channel, thread and history depth.

Next step when it recurs: check the chat turn log for that message. A session
id differing from neighbouring turns points at key resolution (e.g. ThreadID
appearing on one message); history_messages of 0 or 1 with a stable session id
points at the store read path.

Do not close this by guessing. It needs one reproduction with the new log line.

title: Durable scheduled agent tasks backed by Archie's task queue
description: Add first-class one-shot, interval, and cron scheduling for Telegram agents. Due firing uses an atomic lease/idempotency key so concurrent daemons and crash recovery do not duplicate a scheduled occurrence. Scheduler callbacks only enqueue normal tasks; they never run agents or shell commands inline. Each schedule records owner identity, origin chat/thread, prompt/task payload, enabled capability policy, overlap policy, next run, last result, and delivery state. Authorized users can create/list/status/pause/resume/delete/run-now from chat and equivalent typed agent tools. Missed-run, long-running overlap, clock/DST, cancellation, queue failure, execution failure, and delivery failure semantics are explicit and tested with a fake clock. title: Feature-based config: split monolithic config.toml into modular files
description:
Sam's explicit directive: move to feature-based YAML config files in conf.d/ (Linux convention) instead of one monolithic config.toml.

## Design

- ~/.config/archie/config.yaml — daemon-level (work_dir, db_path, poll_interval, max_retries, bot_user, skills_dir, plugin_dir, label, diff_cap_lines, agent, budgets, web, notify, nats, containers, dispatch, forge)
- ~/.config/archie/conf.d/gateway.yaml — chat channels, platform configs
- ~/.config/archie/conf.d/tools.yaml — MCP servers, tool policy
- ~/.config/archie/conf.d/memory.yaml — memory provider config
- ~/.config/archie/conf.d/models.yaml — LLM providers and model role mappings
- ~/.config/archie/conf.d/identities.yaml — identity configs (replaces [[identities]] in TOML)

## Implementation requirements

1. New function: LoadDir(baseDir, overlayDir string) (Config, error)
2. New types on Config: MemoryConfig, ToolsConfig (with MCPServer + ToolPolicy), Extra map[string]any
3. Feature files as top-level YAML keys (memory.yaml has provider, provider_config, session_ttl; tools.yaml has mcp_servers, tool_policy; models.yaml has models, providers, etc.)
4. Legacy support: if config.yaml absent, fall back to config.toml via existing Load function
5. Existing Load() and LoadOverlay() preserved unchanged (they still work with monolithic TOML)
6. Overlay support: overlayDir files merged on top of baseDir files (shallow merge per file, overlay values take precedence, base values inherited for missing keys)
7. Validation: unknown feature files error (prevent typos like config.gaeway.yaml), duplicate feature files error (same name in root and conf.d/), malformed YAML errors
8. Missing feature files mean feature disabled (zero values, no error)
9. YAML parser: gopkg.in/yaml.v3 (already a transitive dependency via NellDB)

## Test contract

28 tests in internal/config/feature_config_test.go define the COMPLETE spec. An implementing agent must:
- NOT modify the test file
- Write implementation that makes all 28 tests pass
- The key signature is: func LoadDir(baseDir, overlayDir string) (Config, error)

## Acceptance
All 28 LoadDir tests pass. Existing Load/LoadOverlay tests pass. go build ./... clean. No config.toml parsing capability is lost.
acceptance_criteria: A new feature (e.g. MCP) can be configured by adding one new TOML file. No changes to existing config parsing code are needed. Legacy monolithic config.toml still works.

description: runFindGoFallback's walk callback swallows every per-entry error (returns nil to skip inaccessible entries), so the only error that can escape filepath.WalkDir is ctx.Err() from the cancellation select. This is the same failure the grep exit-code bug had -- the model is told a search found nothing when the search did not finish. Behaviour predates 6d4e0be; the errors.Is autofix in that commit is behaviour-neutral here (errors.Is(err, nil) is false for non-nil err, matching the old err != ctx.Err() when the context is live).
acceptance_criteria: A find whose context is cancelled mid-walk returns an error result naming the cancellation, not 'no matches found' and not a silently partial list. Regression test in the style of TestGrepReportsSearchFailureRatherThanNoMatches.

title: install.sh: linger detection claims success it did not verify

title: generalize Provider.APIKeyEnv / NATS.TokenEnv / Telegram.TokenEnv to SecretRef
description:
Follow-up to archie-core-xec, which only migrated Forge.TokenEnv (self-contained call site). Provider.APIKeyEnv is forwarded THREE different ways that all assume the secret is reachable by name in the daemon's own env, not resolved centrally:
1. agentexec.NewRuntime -> passes the env-var NAME into ai-sdk/runtime's AuthConfig.APIKeyEnv, which lazily os.Getenv's it later (external module, cannot change its contract).
2. agentexec.WorkerEnvironment / subprocess.go WorkerEnvironment() -> allowlist-forwards the NAME into a subprocess's environment for archie-agent to read itself.
3. daemon.containerEnv() -> already eagerly resolves via os.Getenv and injects NAME=value into a container env (this one generalizes cleanly).

Migrating Provider.APIKeyEnv to SecretRef requires switching cases 1 and 2 from name-forwarding to eager-resolve-via-secret.Registry-then-inject-value (ai-sdk/runtime.AuthConfig.APIKey literal field already supports this per its ResolveAPIKey fallback chain -- no ai-sdk/runtime changes needed, just stop relying on its lazy os.Getenv path for non-env engines). Also migrate NATSConfig.TokenEnv and TelegramConfig.TokenEnv (each has a single simple os.Getenv call site, lower risk than Provider).
design: secret.Registry must be threaded into agentexec.NewRuntime, WorkerEnvironment, and daemon.containerEnv (or a shared secret-resolution helper) so eager-resolve-then-inject replaces name-forwarding for engines other than the built-in env engine.
acceptance_criteria: Provider.APIKeyEnv, NATSConfig.TokenEnv, TelegramConfig.TokenEnv replaced with SecretRef; all three consumption paths (in-process runtime, subprocess worker env, container env) resolve via secret.Registry; task check passes; adversarial review finds zero surviving findings; explicit test proving a non-env engine (e.g. a fake test engine) correctly delivers a provider API key to agentexec.NewRuntime via the AuthConfig.APIKey literal field, not APIKeyEnv.
notes:
Hit this while implementing archie-core-rs9 (TOML write strategy for `archied setup`). The parent epic archie-core-ewk / child archie-core-cbk describe setup step 2 (LLM provider) and step 5 (chat channel) as writing the credential "via the secret engine" -- i.e. a general {engine,key} SecretRef, same as Forge.Token. That's not accurate yet: as this bead already says, Provider.APIKeyEnv and Telegram.TokenEnv are plain env-var-name strings with no Registry involved, so today they can only ever mean the built-in "env" engine, whatever setup writes into them.

Practical effect on archie-core-cbk: until this migrates, cbk's provider and chat-channel steps should either (a) only support the env engine for those two fields and say so explicitly when prompting, or (b) block on this bead if full multi-engine secret support is a hard requirement for setup. I did not attempt to fix this myself -- out of scope for rs9, and this bead already scopes the real fix (thread secret.Registry into agentexec.NewRuntime/WorkerEnvironment and daemon side). Flagging so whoever picks up cbk decides (a) vs (b) deliberately rather than discovering it mid-implementation.

Adversarially reviewed with all findings fixed and regression-tested -- DONE.
notes:
Adversarial review (fresh agent) found 5 real findings, all fixed:
1. HIGH - path traversal: server-supplied tool name (from tools/list, untrusted) was used directly in filepath.Join(mediaDir, toolName) with no sanitization -- a malicious MCP server could advertise a tool named e.g. '../../../etc/cron.d/evil' and write attacker-controlled bytes outside mediaDir. Fixed: rejectPathTraversal() rejects any tool name containing a path separator or being exactly '.'/'..' before it's used as a path component; tested (TestCallToolHandlerRejectsPathTraversalToolName, TestWriteMultimodalResultRejectsDotAndDotDotToolNames).
2. MEDIUM - no size cap on base64 media before decode+write: unbounded memory/disk exhaustion from a misbehaving server. Fixed: maxMediaBlockBase64Bytes (64MiB) checked before decode; tested (TestWriteMultimodalResultRejectsOversizedMediaBlock).
3. MEDIUM - concurrent calls to the same tool used index-only filenames in a shared per-tool directory, so two concurrent calls could write to the same path and clobber/interleave each other's files. 4. **DeadTargetRegistry**: Persistent JSON tracking of confirmed-dead targets (deleted groups, kicked bots). Self-healing on successful send.
5. **Wake delivery**: Use NATS request/reply for async delivery to push-capable adapters.
acceptance_criteria: A cron job can schedule a message for delivery. If the target is unreachable, the ledger retries. If the bot is kicked from a group, the target is registered dead and skipped.

title: daemon.go: hand off whole task to archie-agent in sandboxed NATS+container mode
description: Depends on the archie-agent full-task handler existing. internal/daemon/daemon.go's process() currently always calls workflow.Route/workflow.Run itself, dispatching per-stage LLM calls to d.Agent (NATSRunner does this over NATS today). When d.Nats != nil && d.ContainerPool != nil (the sandboxed path this whole PRD phase targets), process() should instead publish one 'run whole task' message to archie-agent and await its completion report, skipping local workflow.Route/workflow.Run entirely. inprocess/subprocess modes (no container pool) keep calling workflow.Run in the daemon exactly as today — this only changes behavior for the fully-sandboxed path.
acceptance_criteria: With containers enabled, daemon.process() delegates the entire task to archie-agent in one round trip; without containers, behavior is unchanged (verified by existing daemon tests continuing to pass).
close_reason: daemon.process() now branches on d.ContainerPool != nil: sandboxed tasks get handed to archie-agent via a new runViaAgent method (publishes taskrun.Request to archie.taskrun.<id>, awaits taskrun.Response) instead of calling workflow.Route/workflow.Run locally; non-container mode is unchanged. runViaAgent only parks the task itself on transport/setup failure (encode error, no responder, decode error, or an error returned before archie-agent's workflow.Run got to run) — on success, every durable side effect already landed via the storerpc/forgerpc/worktreerpc proxies during archie-agent's run, so runViaAgent just logs. Added agentexec.ProvidersFromConfig (deduped from cmd/archied's former executionProviders). Also fixed a real correctness gap this surfaced: with concurrent multi-task dispatch (u64/g1l) plus containerized archie-agent, the 5zh.7 wildcard queue-group subscription could let one container answer a sibling's taskrun message despite having a different task's worktree mounted. archie-agent now reads its boot-time task.json (container.TaskPayload, already written by daemon.process() before container acquire) and subscribes to its own exact archie.taskrun.<id> subject when present, falling back to the shared queue group only when no task.json exists (dev/pool mode). Full container-mode integration (real Docker) isn't covered by an automated test, consistent with the rest of the container-dependent code — runViaAgent itself is unit-tested directly against embedded NATS, bypassing the Docker-dependent Acquire path. This closes the archie-core-5zh epic: archie-agent now runs an entire task's workflow per invocation instead of one stage per round trip, with Store/Forge/git-push credentials staying daemon-side throughout.

title: Scale-to-zero: idle detection and dormant quiesce
description:
Scale-to-zero idle detection:

1. **Idle predicate**: running_agent_count == 0 AND seconds_since_last_inbound > idle_timeout AND no live background work.
2. **Dormant transition**: Signal relay transport to close socket (supervisor preserved).
3. **Wake trigger**: Inbound message on wake URL resumes gateway.
4. **Structural precondition**: Only arms when messaging is relay-only or absent AND a wake URL is registered.

Ref: docs/prds/hermes-gap-analysis.md section 6 (scale_to_zero.py)

title: Eliminate intermittent JetStream TempDir teardown race
description:
An intermittent full-suite race failure shows TestConnectAndPublish cleaning its testing.TempDir while JetStream is still removing the ARCHIE_TASKS msgs directory. The package subsequently passed five race iterations, so the timing window is narrow.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run: go test -race -count=1 ./...
2. Repeat until internal/nats TestConnectAndPublish fails during TempDir RemoveAll with: unlinkat .../jetstream/$G/streams/ARCHIE_TASKS/msgs: directory not empty.
3. Compare with: go test -race -count=5 ./internal/nats.

Make embedded NATS shutdown and storage cleanup deterministic before TempDir cleanup.
acceptance_criteria: Repeated race runs of internal/nats and the full repository do not race TempDir cleanup against JetStream file removal; the test explicitly waits for server/storage shutdown.
close_reason: Fixed the JetStream TempDir teardown race by: (1) Moving t.Cleanup registration AFTER t.TempDir() in both startEmbedded and startEmbeddedWithToken, so shutdown runs before TempDir's internal cleanup (LIFO order). (2) Using srv.Shutdown() + srv.WaitForShutdown() instead of bare srv.Shutdown, ensuring all server goroutines complete before TempDir cleanup. Verified with go test -race -count=10 ./internal/nats/ and full go test -race ./... both passing consistently.

title: Persistent volumes with TTL for container/worktree storage
description: Phase 2 of docs/prds/archie-core-v2-architecture.md. Current worktree lifecycle is fresh-clone-per-task with status-driven cleanup, no TTL. Add persistent volume support with TTL-based expiry to avoid repeated full clones for repeated work on the same repo.

notes: Implemented containers.volume_ttl (72h default, negative rejected); per-repo bare Git object caches seed dissociated issue worktrees when persistent_storage is enabled; Archie-owned repo Docker volumes are labeled and automatically reaped by age without touching cache/unowned volumes; daemon startup and cycles reap both storage layers; config example and v2 PRD updated. Validation: focused race tests count=5 passed for config/storage/worktree/daemon; go vet ./... passed; scoped staticcheck passed; gofumpt clean; go build ./... passed; full go test -race -count=1 ./... passed on repeat. Repository-wide golangci-lint remains red on 39 pre-existing findings tracked by archie-core-756. One non-reproducing NATS TempDir cleanup flake tracked by archie-core-340 after internal/nats passed race count=5.
close_reason: Persistent container/worktree storage now has configured TTL expiry. Repos opting into persistent_storage retain an Archie-owned Docker repo volume and reuse a per-repo bare Git object cache to avoid repeated full network clones while keeping issue worktrees isolated via dissociated clones. containers.volume_ttl defaults to 72h; daemon startup/cycles automatically remove expired owned repo volumes and Git caches. Tests cover config default/validation, Docker ownership labels and selective expiry, cache reuse/isolation/expiry/path safety, and daemon TTL wiring. Full race suite, vet, build, formatting, and scoped staticcheck pass.
